enzymes.why_it_matters: Direct electron transfer between the metal surface and the enzyme, shown to accelerate mild-steel corrosion. blocking_problems.what_would_settle_it: Residual activity of the purified enzyme after exposure to air at the dissolved-oxygen tension of subcutaneous tissue. blocking_problems.detail: One mole of H2 per mole of iron, inside a closed capsule. See hydrogen_evolution() for the volume; it is millilitres, not microlitres.
blocking_problems.severity: needs a number before it needs a solution
blocking_problems.what_would_settle_it: Whether diffusion out beats production. H2 is the smallest molecule there is, so it may never accumulate -- but the total is fixed by the mass balance and has to be compared against it.

blocking_problems.problem: It releases Fe(II), the dangerous oxidation state

blocking_problems.severity: same constraint as the rest of the arm
blocking_problems.what_would_settle_it: Nothing new -- it is the chelator ceiling already computed here.

refs.title: Composition and toxicity of shrapnel in mine-explosive and fragmentation craniocerebral wounds compared to titanium implants
refs.says: Twelve projectiles removed from brain tissue were analysed by SEM with X-ray microanalysis; three were ferromagnetic and were taken forward for composition and cytotoxicity against a human cell line. Ferrous fragments in the head are not a hypothetical case.

stainless.why_not: Stainless is passivating, and that single fact moves it out of this arm and in beside aluminium and titanium. At or above about 10.5% chromium the alloy grows a Cr2O3 film a few nanometres thick that is dense rather than flaky, adherent rather than spalling, and re-forms within seconds wherever it is scratched. The whole iron route depends on the opposite behaviour: rust flakes, fresh metal is exposed, tissue re-oxidises it, and the chelator takes the next layer. Against Cr2O3 there is no next layer. Deferoxamine is also selective for Fe(III) and does not meaningfully lift chromium oxide, so the chelator that drives the carbon-steel route does nothing here.
stainless.clinical_consequence: A surgeon cannot tell carbon steel from stainless by looking at a radiograph, and this engine was treating them as one material. They are not one material: the same treatment that slowly debulks a carbon-steel fragment does nothing at all to a stainless bearing. Any trial has to establish fragment composition as an inclusion criterion, not discover it afterwards.
stainless.how_to_tell: Retrieved fragments go to XRF or SEM-EDS, which is routine and fast. In situ it is harder: dual-energy CT separates some alloys, and a stainless fragment is usually less MRI-hostile than a carbon-steel one because many bearing grades are austenitic and only weakly magnetic. Neither is definitive, and the honest position is that composition is unknown before retrieval.

blocking_problems.detail: One mole of H2 per mole of iron, inside a closed capsule. See hydrogen_evolution() for the volume; it is millilitres, not microlitres.
blocking_problems.severity: needs a number before it needs a solution

blocking_problems.problem: It releases Fe(II), the dangerous oxidation state

blocking_problems.severity: same constraint as the rest of the arm
blocking_problems.what_would_settle_it: Nothing new -- it is the chelator ceiling already computed here.

stages.what: Pull Fe(III) off the oxide surface with a high-affinity chelator, with ascorbate as a reductant alongside it.
stages.why: Nothing is added to make the fragment rust. Dissolution is driven by removing the product: strip Fe(III) from the surface and the equilibrium pulls more off behind it. stages.self_limiting: This is the property that answers the arm's own warning. steel.target: Match capacity to the fragment, by mass balance
steel.detail: A 24-subunit shell holds on the order of thousands of iron atoms. The fragment's mass gives the moles of iron exactly, as it does for a polymer, so the number of shells needed is arithmetic rather than an estimate. This is the calculation to do first, because if it comes out absurd the route is dead before any biology is attempted.

steel.target: Decide whether the enzyme is needed at all
steel.detail: At pH 7.4 Fe(II) autoxidises in air within minutes. If the uncatalysed reaction already outpaces the enzyme, ferritin's value is entirely in the storing and none of it in the oxidising -- which would make this a chelation problem with a protein-shaped container, and would simplify the programme. Measure before engineering.

steel.target: Keep the shell from unloading in tissue
steel.detail: Ferritin releases iron on demand in a cell; here it must not. Stabilising the loaded shell, or clearing it before it is asked to release, is the safety question that replaces the old pH problem.

steel.target: Keep Cyc2 as the rate option, not the lead

clinical_precedents.but: It degrades hyaluronic acid, which is the carrier backbone in the team's hydrogel design. An HA gel in tissue meets host hyaluronidase whether or not anyone injects more.

clinical_precedents.proves: An injected OXIDOREDUCTASE, used to change a substrate's oxidation state fast. This is the regulatory analogue a ferroxidase arm needed and did not have.
clinical_precedents.but: Systemic, and its substrate is a dissolved metabolite rather than a solid.

clinical_precedents.but: Carries a boxed warning for anaphylaxis, which is the honest price of a microbial enzyme in a human.

clinical_precedents.proves: Local delivery to a compartment with low systemic exposure, which is the depot argument.

burden.reason: NR has no fixed repeat-unit mass at the polymer-class level, so the released molar quantity cannot be bounded from mass alone. The fragment's own composition has to be characterised first.

indication.problem: A retained fragment is not inert. Lead from retained bullets causes systemic toxicity that is real but underdiagnosed, and is typically recognised months to years after the injury.

ref.title: Retained bullets and lead toxicity: a systematic review
ref.says: 142 articles. Lead toxicity from retained fragments is real but underdiagnosed, diagnosed months to years after the wound, and driven by fragment location, number and dwell time -- fragments in a fluid compartment carry the highest risk. No consensus exists on when to operate, and chelation alone is not an alternative to removal.

risk_factors: Fragments sitting in a fluid compartment, such as a joint space, carry substantially higher risk.
Risk rises with the number of fragments, an associated fracture, and how long the fragment has been in place.
indication.why_a_gap_exists: The same review found no consensus on when to monitor, chelate or operate, and concluded that long-term chelation is not a substitute for removal. That is the space this product is aimed at: fragments where surgery is the only established answer and the approach itself is the risk.
indication.honest_limit: This evidence is about lead. It establishes that retained fragments can harm and that removal is sometimes the only option, not that an enzymatic route is the right alternative, and not anything about the polymer fragments this engine selects catalysts for.

missing_experiment.question: Does a PET hydrolase cut any bonds at all on a solid fragment at 37 C in serum, at the crystallinity of real debris?
missing_experiment.why_it_is_a_gate: It is a yes/no question that costs months, and everything downstream is wasted effort if the answer is no. A programme that spends its first year on protein engineering before asking it finds out in its third.
missing_experiment.what_not_to_ask_for: They assume a dissolved substrate at a known molar concentration, and a fragment has a surface rather than a [S]. Asking for them on a solid sends someone to a bench to produce a number that cannot be defined, which is worse than asking for nothing. The quantity that does exist is interfacial: rate per unit area, adsorbed enzyme density, and bonds cut per adsorption event.

method_exists.what: Single-molecule fluorescence on probe-doped polymer nanoparticles already resolves interfacial PET hydrolysis, including semi-processive cutting within one adsorption event and an effective reaction distance near 2 nm.

ref.title: Single-molecule detection of enzymatic PET hydrolysis using fluorogenic probe-doped PET nanoparticles
ref.says: Resolves PET hydrolysis at a solid interface one molecule at a time: enzymes cut several bonds per adsorption event, with an effective reaction distance near 2 nm. Cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition while the bulk rate keeps rising -- the physics that makes 37 C hard, and the method for measuring it.

why_unstudied: The field's incentive is recycling, not medicine. PET hydrolase work targets 60-70 C, near the polymer's glass transition, where chains are mobile. 37 C has no commercial value for recycling, so it is not a gap in knowledge so much as a gap in the question.
Michaelis-Menten does not transfer to a solid, so the field measures on soluble model esters where it does. Interfacial kinetics is a different methodological tradition.

The physics at 37 C is genuinely unfavourable: cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition, and below it the chains are not moving. A negative result there is also not a publication anyone chases.

reason_for_optimism.what: Degradation efficiency across a set of bio-polyesters tracked the conformational match between polymer chain and enzyme 'regardless of the actual reaction temperature employed'. If conformational fit matters more than thermal energy, the barrier at 37 C may be lower than the glass-transition argument alone suggests. That is the hypothesis the experiment tests.

ref.title: Conformational selection in enzyme-catalyzed depolymerization of bio-based polyesters
ref.says: Gauche and trans chain conformers, which belong to crystalline and amorphous regions, bind PETase with different affinity. Degradation efficiency tracked the conformational match between polymer and enzyme regardless of the reaction temperature used.

residue.open: Where coated residue finally goes is partly answered. The tattoo-pigment literature, often cited here, shows pigment cycling between macrophages in place and does not demonstrate clearance. Drainage to regional nodes is documented for colloidal particles injected subcutaneously, and PEGylation increases it -- but that is subcutaneous tissue, not deep muscle, and arriving in a node is where those studies stop looking. missing_experiment.question: Does a PET hydrolase cut any bonds at all on a solid fragment at 37 C in serum, at the crystallinity of real debris?
missing_experiment.why_it_is_a_gate: It is a yes/no question that costs months, and everything downstream is wasted effort if the answer is no. A programme that spends its first year on protein engineering before asking it finds out in its third.
missing_experiment.what_not_to_ask_for: They assume a dissolved substrate at a known molar concentration, and a fragment has a surface rather than a [S]. Asking for them on a solid sends someone to a bench to produce a number that cannot be defined, which is worse than asking for nothing. The quantity that does exist is interfacial: rate per unit area, adsorbed enzyme density, and bonds cut per adsorption event.

method_exists.what: Single-molecule fluorescence on probe-doped polymer nanoparticles already resolves interfacial PET hydrolysis, including semi-processive cutting within one adsorption event and an effective reaction distance near 2 nm.

ref.title: Single-molecule detection of enzymatic PET hydrolysis using fluorogenic probe-doped PET nanoparticles

why_unstudied: The field's incentive is recycling, not medicine. PET hydrolase work targets 60-70 C, near the polymer's glass transition, where chains are mobile. 37 C has no commercial value for recycling, so it is not a gap in knowledge so much as a gap in the question.
Michaelis-Menten does not transfer to a solid, so the field measures on soluble model esters where it does. Interfacial kinetics is a different methodological tradition.

The physics at 37 C is genuinely unfavourable: cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition, and below it the chains are not moving. A negative result there is also not a publication anyone chases.

indication.problem: A retained fragment is not inert. Lead from retained bullets causes systemic toxicity that is real but underdiagnosed, and is typically recognised months to years after the injury.

ref.title: Retained bullets and lead toxicity: a systematic review
ref.says: 142 articles. Lead toxicity from retained fragments is real but underdiagnosed, diagnosed months to years after the wound, and driven by fragment location, number and dwell time -- fragments in a fluid compartment carry the highest risk. No consensus exists on when to operate, and chelation alone is not an alternative to removal.

risk_factors: Fragments sitting in a fluid compartment, such as a joint space, carry substantially higher risk.
Risk rises with the number of fragments, an associated fracture, and how long the fragment has been in place.
indication.why_a_gap_exists: The same review found no consensus on when to monitor, chelate or operate, and concluded that long-term chelation is not a substitute for removal. That is the space this product is aimed at: fragments where surgery is the only established answer and the approach itself is the risk.
indication.honest_limit: This evidence is about lead. It establishes that retained fragments can harm and that removal is sometimes the only option, not that an enzymatic route is the right alternative, and not anything about the polymer fragments this engine selects catalysts for.

missing_experiment.question: Does a PET hydrolase cut any bonds at all on a solid fragment at 37 C in serum, at the crystallinity of real debris?
missing_experiment.why_it_is_a_gate: It is a yes/no question that costs months, and everything downstream is wasted effort if the answer is no. A programme that spends its first year on protein engineering before asking it finds out in its third.
missing_experiment.what_not_to_ask_for: They assume a dissolved substrate at a known molar concentration, and a fragment has a surface rather than a [S]. Asking for them on a solid sends someone to a bench to produce a number that cannot be defined, which is worse than asking for nothing. The quantity that does exist is interfacial: rate per unit area, adsorbed enzyme density, and bonds cut per adsorption event.

method_exists.what: Single-molecule fluorescence on probe-doped polymer nanoparticles already resolves interfacial PET hydrolysis, including semi-processive cutting within one adsorption event and an effective reaction distance near 2 nm.

ref.title: Single-molecule detection of enzymatic PET hydrolysis using fluorogenic probe-doped PET nanoparticles
ref.says: Resolves PET hydrolysis at a solid interface one molecule at a time: enzymes cut several bonds per adsorption event, with an effective reaction distance near 2 nm. Cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition while the bulk rate keeps rising -- the physics that makes 37 C hard, and the method for measuring it.

why_unstudied: The field's incentive is recycling, not medicine. PET hydrolase work targets 60-70 C, near the polymer's glass transition, where chains are mobile. 37 C has no commercial value for recycling, so it is not a gap in knowledge so much as a gap in the question.
Michaelis-Menten does not transfer to a solid, so the field measures on soluble model esters where it does. Interfacial kinetics is a different methodological tradition.

The physics at 37 C is genuinely unfavourable: cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition, and below it the chains are not moving. A negative result there is also not a publication anyone chases.

reason_for_optimism.what: Degradation efficiency across a set of bio-polyesters tracked the conformational match between polymer chain and enzyme 'regardless of the actual reaction temperature employed'. If conformational fit matters more than thermal energy, the barrier at 37 C may be lower than the glass-transition argument alone suggests. That is the hypothesis the experiment tests.

ref.says: Gauche and trans chain conformers, which belong to crystalline and amorphous regions, bind PETase with different affinity. Degradation efficiency tracked the conformational match between polymer and enzyme regardless of the reaction temperature used.

missing_experiment.question: Does a PET hydrolase cut any bonds at all on a solid fragment at 37 C in serum, at the crystallinity of real debris?
missing_experiment.why_it_is_a_gate: It is a yes/no question that costs months, and everything downstream is wasted effort if the answer is no. A programme that spends its first year on protein engineering before asking it finds out in its third.
missing_experiment.what_not_to_ask_for: They assume a dissolved substrate at a known molar concentration, and a fragment has a surface rather than a [S]. Asking for them on a solid sends someone to a bench to produce a number that cannot be defined, which is worse than asking for nothing. The quantity that does exist is interfacial: rate per unit area, adsorbed enzyme density, and bonds cut per adsorption event.

method_exists.what: Single-molecule fluorescence on probe-doped polymer nanoparticles already resolves interfacial PET hydrolysis, including semi-processive cutting within one adsorption event and an effective reaction distance near 2 nm.

ref.title: Single-molecule detection of enzymatic PET hydrolysis using fluorogenic probe-doped PET nanoparticles
ref.says: Resolves PET hydrolysis at a solid interface one molecule at a time: enzymes cut several bonds per adsorption event, with an effective reaction distance near 2 nm. Cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition while the bulk rate keeps rising -- the physics that makes 37 C hard, and the method for measuring it.

why_unstudied: The field's incentive is recycling, not medicine. PET hydrolase work targets 60-70 C, near the polymer's glass transition, where chains are mobile. 37 C has no commercial value for recycling, so it is not a gap in knowledge so much as a gap in the question.
Michaelis-Menten does not transfer to a solid, so the field measures on soluble model esters where it does. Interfacial kinetics is a different methodological tradition.

The physics at 37 C is genuinely unfavourable: cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition, and below it the chains are not moving. A negative result there is also not a publication anyone chases.

missing_experiment.question: Does a PET hydrolase cut any bonds at all on a solid fragment at 37 C in serum, at the crystallinity of real debris?
missing_experiment.why_it_is_a_gate: It is a yes/no question that costs months, and everything downstream is wasted effort if the answer is no. A programme that spends its first year on protein engineering before asking it finds out in its third.
missing_experiment.what_not_to_ask_for: They assume a dissolved substrate at a known molar concentration, and a fragment has a surface rather than a [S]. Asking for them on a solid sends someone to a bench to produce a number that cannot be defined, which is worse than asking for nothing. The quantity that does exist is interfacial: rate per unit area, adsorbed enzyme density, and bonds cut per adsorption event.

method_exists.what: Single-molecule fluorescence on probe-doped polymer nanoparticles already resolves interfacial PET hydrolysis, including semi-processive cutting within one adsorption event and an effective reaction distance near 2 nm.

ref.title: Single-molecule detection of enzymatic PET hydrolysis using fluorogenic probe-doped PET nanoparticles
ref.says: Resolves PET hydrolysis at a solid interface one molecule at a time: enzymes cut several bonds per adsorption event, with an effective reaction distance near 2 nm. why_unstudied: The field's incentive is recycling, not medicine. PET hydrolase work targets 60-70 C, near the polymer's glass transition, where chains are mobile. 37 C has no commercial value for recycling, so it is not a gap in knowledge so much as a gap in the question.
Michaelis-Menten does not transfer to a solid, so the field measures on soluble model esters where it does. Interfacial kinetics is a different methodological tradition.

The physics at 37 C is genuinely unfavourable: cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition, and below it the chains are not moving. A negative result there is also not a publication anyone chases.

indication.problem: A retained fragment is not inert. Lead from retained bullets causes systemic toxicity that is real but underdiagnosed, and is typically recognised months to years after the injury.

ref.title: Retained bullets and lead toxicity: a systematic review
ref.says: 142 articles. Lead toxicity from retained fragments is real but underdiagnosed, diagnosed months to years after the wound, and driven by fragment location, number and dwell time -- fragments in a fluid compartment carry the highest risk. No consensus exists on when to operate, and chelation alone is not an alternative to removal.

risk_factors: Fragments sitting in a fluid compartment, such as a joint space, carry substantially higher risk.
Risk rises with the number of fragments, an associated fracture, and how long the fragment has been in place.
indication.why_a_gap_exists: The same review found no consensus on when to monitor, chelate or operate, and concluded that long-term chelation is not a substitute for removal. That is the space this product is aimed at: fragments where surgery is the only established answer and the approach itself is the risk.
indication.honest_limit: This evidence is about lead. It establishes that retained fragments can harm and that removal is sometimes the only option, not that an enzymatic route is the right alternative, and not anything about the polymer fragments this engine selects catalysts for.

missing_experiment.question: Does a PET hydrolase cut any bonds at all on a solid fragment at 37 C in serum, at the crystallinity of real debris?
missing_experiment.why_it_is_a_gate: It is a yes/no question that costs months, and everything downstream is wasted effort if the answer is no. A programme that spends its first year on protein engineering before asking it finds out in its third.
missing_experiment.what_not_to_ask_for: They assume a dissolved substrate at a known molar concentration, and a fragment has a surface rather than a [S]. Asking for them on a solid sends someone to a bench to produce a number that cannot be defined, which is worse than asking for nothing. The quantity that does exist is interfacial: rate per unit area, adsorbed enzyme density, and bonds cut per adsorption event.

method_exists.what: Single-molecule fluorescence on probe-doped polymer nanoparticles already resolves interfacial PET hydrolysis, including semi-processive cutting within one adsorption event and an effective reaction distance near 2 nm.

ref.title: Single-molecule detection of enzymatic PET hydrolysis using fluorogenic probe-doped PET nanoparticles
ref.says: Resolves PET hydrolysis at a solid interface one molecule at a time: enzymes cut several bonds per adsorption event, with an effective reaction distance near 2 nm. Cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition while the bulk rate keeps rising -- the physics that makes 37 C hard, and the method for measuring it.

why_unstudied: The field's incentive is recycling, not medicine. PET hydrolase work targets 60-70 C, near the polymer's glass transition, where chains are mobile. 37 C has no commercial value for recycling, so it is not a gap in knowledge so much as a gap in the question.
Michaelis-Menten does not transfer to a solid, so the field measures on soluble model esters where it does. Interfacial kinetics is a different methodological tradition.

The physics at 37 C is genuinely unfavourable: cutting frequency tracks surface-chain mobility near the glass transition, and below it the chains are not moving. A negative result there is also not a publication anyone chases.

reason_for_optimism.what: Degradation efficiency across a set of bio-polyesters tracked the conformational match between polymer chain and enzyme 'regardless of the actual reaction temperature employed'. If conformational fit matters more than thermal energy, the barrier at 37 C may be lower than the glass-transition argument alone suggests. That is the hypothesis the experiment tests.

ref.title: Conformational selection in enzyme-catalyzed depolymerization of bio-based polyesters
ref.says: Gauche and trans chain conformers, which belong to crystalline and amorphous regions, bind PETase with different affinity. Degradation efficiency tracked the conformational match between polymer and enzyme regardless of the reaction temperature used.

residue.open: Where coated residue finally goes is partly answered. The tattoo-pigment literature, often cited here, shows pigment cycling between macrophages in place and does not demonstrate clearance. Drainage to regional nodes is documented for colloidal particles injected subcutaneously, and PEGylation increases it -- but that is subcutaneous tissue, not deep muscle, and arriving in a node is where those studies stop looking. Whether residue reaches a node from muscle, and what it does once there, are two separate measurements and neither has been made.

caveats.detail: The originally cited work varied size and shape, not modulus, and found larger spheres provoked less fibrosis -- it cannot carry a stiffness claim. The mechanism does have support: macrophage TRPV4 reads matrix stiffness and drives TGF-beta activation, and deleting it in myeloid cells protects mice from fibrosis. That was measured in lung fibrosis, not against an implant, and a review of mechanical cues in the foreign-body reaction reports the polarisation results as inconsistent between studies. So: plausible mechanism, real evidence, not yet demonstrated for this application.
